mappings.note: Two parasitic organisms, and how fungi feed. Both are heterotrophic nutrition modes, C 3.2-LO-1.

DEFECT: two unrelated items have been merged into one stem -- a statement about saprotrophs pouring out digestive enzymes, then David's leaf-peel observation. The saprotroph half is C 3.2-LO-1; the stored answer (epidermal cells and guard cells) puts the observation half at C 3.1. Both cited because the row carries two questions.
When clotting is useful, and the four events of clotting as a flow chart. Blood within the human transport system, C 3.2-LO-2.

Three reasons asked. The epiglottis over the glottis and the cartilage rings in the trachea are respiratory-pathway organs (C 3.2-LO-2); alveoli being wrapped in capillaries is the alveolus structure serving gas exchange (C 4.2-LO-1). Split deliberately rather than forcing all three into one code.
What double circulation is and why it is necessary. Same as qid:85623 and qid:85661; C 3.2-LO-2.
What stomata are, a labelled diagram, and two functions. The functions are gas exchange and transpiration (the exchange strand of C 3.2); the labelled structure is the guard-cell pair (C 3.1).
Names photosynthesis, lists its three events, and asks for two nitrogen sources for plants. All autotrophic nutrition, C 3.2-LO-1.
Final products of digesting carbohydrate, protein and fat -- C 3.2-LO-1.
Why a sportsman gets cramps -- lactic acid from anaerobic respiration in muscle. Products of anaerobic respiration, C 3.2-LO-3.

Mouth pH below 5.5: what changes and how to control it. Like qid:85747 the assessed science is acid attack on enamel (C 1.3), sitting in a digestion bank (C 3.2-LO-1). Really Acids, Bases and Salts content.

Three parts: breathing rhythmic vs gas exchange continuous, and a leak in the circulatory tubes, are both human transport/respiration (C 3.2-LO-2); stomatal opening and closing is guard-cell turgor (C 3.1).
A bear has lost much of its small intestine -- recommend a plant or meat diet. Reasoning from gut length to nutrition strategy, the same idea as qid:85654, C 3.2-LO-1.
Name the site of complete digestion and explain the process -- the human nutrition sequence, C 3.2-LO-1.
Three kinds of blood vessel and their functions -- C 3.2-LO-2.
Three digestive glands and their secretions -- C 3.2-LO-1, the fuller version of qid:85733.
Three differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration -- C 3.2-LO-3.

Haemoglobin and the cell holding it is transport (C 3.2-LO-2); the lactic-acid product of oxygen-starved muscle and the fermentation-vs-aerobic end products are C 3.2-LO-3. The item deliberately straddles both.
Roles of pepsin, saliva, villi and bile. Three are digestive secretions (C 3.2-LO-1); the villus is one of the three structures C 4.2-LO-1 names, so it is cited too.
Roles of the stomach wall muscles, hydrochloric acid and mucus -- all steps of human digestion, C 3.2-LO-1.
Why transpiration matters, and why plants wilt in the afternoon but recover overnight. Both are xylem water relations, C 4.3-LO-1.
The form in which plants take nitrogen, and the nutrition type of bread mould. Autotrophic raw materials and a saprophytic mode -- both C 3.2-LO-1.
Distinguishes excretion from elimination, then asks for excretory organs across VERTEBRATES. The cross-species scope puts it at the competency C 3.2; LO-2 covers excretion in human beings only.
Why diffusion is insufficient in humans and what arrangement large animals use instead. The body-organisation argument, C 4.2, consistent with qid:85594 and qid:85636.

A blood-donation scenario asking for blood composition and O2/CO2 transport (C 3.2-LO-2) and then for the values Mohan's group displayed. That last part is Science in human life viewed through ethics, which is exactly C 5.2 -- the one place in this frame where a values question has a home.

Functions of bile, and why the pancreas is both endocrine and exocrine. Both are digestive glands within human nutrition, C 3.2-LO-1; the endocrine mention is incidental and this chapter's frame has no hormone outcome.
180 litres filtered but only 1.5 litres excreted -- selective reabsorption. Human excretory pathway, C 3.2-LO-2.
Site of complete digestion, which two organs feed the small intestine, and which secretes trypsin. All C 3.2-LO-1.
Three features making the lungs an efficient respiratory surface -- alveolar surface area, thin walls, rich blood supply. Structure serving function, C 4.2-LO-1.
How Amoeba captures food and what its nutrition mode is -- C 3.2-LO-1.
What translocation is, why it is essential, and where phloem delivers. Plant transport, C 4.3-LO-1.
Why chewed bread tastes sweet (salivary amylase), and why cellulose is roughage for us but food for a cow. Both are nutrition, C 3.2-LO-1.
Why transport of materials is necessary in animals at all. This is the need-for-a-system argument rather than a description of the system, so C 4.2 rather than C 3.2-LO-2.
One function each for blood vessels, lymph and heart -- the components of human transport, C 3.2-LO-2.

DEFECT: this row is not a question -- the title is the heading 'Three Kinds of Blood Cells' followed by a list. The stored answer gives the functions of RBCs, WBCs and platelets, so the content is blood as the transport medium: C 3.2-LO-2. Mapped on content, but the row needs a stem.
Why diffusion suffices for a single cell but not for a multicellular body. The same body-organisation argument as qid:85789, C 4.2.
Cartilage rings, the alveolar sac and the voice box are respiratory-pathway anatomy (C 3.2-LO-2); why plants look green is chlorophyll in the chloroplast (C 3.1). Two unrelated halves in one row.

The experiment showing an atmospheric gas is essential for photosynthesis: name the gas, say what the watch glass holds and why, predict the difference between pots a and b. Content is autotrophic nutrition (C 3.2-LO-1); the KOH control and the paired-pot comparison are C 8.1 variable manipulation.
How water and minerals are transported in plants. Duplicate of qid:85609; C 4.3-LO-1.
Why mouth-breathing is harmful and what makes nasal breathing safer -- filtration and warming in the nasal passage, part of the human respiratory pathway, C 3.2-LO-2.
Activity showing chlorophyll is essential for photosynthesis (variegated leaf and starch test). Autotrophic nutrition plus controlled-variable experimental design.
Define excretion and give two vital kidney functions. Framed on the human excretory organ, so C 3.2-LO-2 rather than the cross-species competency used for qid:85788.
Compare alveoli and nephrons in structure and functioning. Duplicate of qid:85625; C 4.2-LO-1 names both structures.
Structure of the bronchi with trachea and bronchiole labelled -- respiratory-pathway anatomy, C 3.2-LO-2. Not C 4.2-LO-1: the bronchus is not one of the three structures that outcome names.
Name three life processes essential for maintaining life and explain one. Asks across the processes, so the competency C 3.2; which LO would apply depends on which process the candidate picks.
How autotrophs meet their energy needs and the form unused carbohydrate takes (starch). Autotrophic nutrition and its storage product, C 3.2-LO-1.
Why digestion is essential, and the storage form of food energy. C 3.2-LO-1, matching qid:85717.
Activity with diagram showing carbon dioxide is essential for photosynthesis -- content C 3.2-LO-1, experimental design C 8.1.
Three reasons transpiration is significant -- C 4.3-LO-1, as for qid:85673 and qid:85743.

Why both plants and animals need special transport tissues or organs. A body-organisation argument spanning both kingdoms, so C 4.2 rather than either the plant (C 4.3-LO-1) or human (C 3.2-LO-2) transport outcome.

A nitrogenous waste in urine, the name of the kidney's basic unit, and how urine volume is regulated. Human excretory pathway, C 3.2-LO-2; naming the nephron is not enough to make it the structure-function outcome C 4.2-LO-1.

Three features common to the respiratory organs of ANIMALS generally -- thin, moist, vascular, large-surfaced. C 4.2-LO-1 names only the alveolus, nephron and villus, and LO-2 is human-only, so the competency C 3.2 is the right level for a cross-animal generalisation.
Structure and function of the nephron -- C 4.2-LO-1 names the nephron and asks precisely for structure related to function.

Holozoic vs saprophytic nutrition with examples, the roles of liver and pancreas, which organ absorbs food and which water, and why bile matters without enzymes. Every part is human or heterotrophic nutrition, C 3.2-LO-1.
Part (a) labels the alimentary canal and names its longest part (C 3.2-LO-1); part (b) asks why oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept separate (C 3.2-LO-2). Two processes bolted into one row.
Three events of photosynthesis and the role of stomata, then an experiment showing sunlight is essential. Content plus experimental design, so C 3.2-LO-1 with C 8.1.
Labelling the alimentary canal's glands and absorptive part is C 3.2-LO-1; 'what are villi and what do they do' is the villus structure-to-function outcome C 4.2-LO-1.
Leaf cross-section labels include the chloroplast and the question asks for the site of photosynthesis (C 3.1); defining photosynthesis, its events, equation and storage form is C 3.2-LO-1.
Alimentary-canal labels, emulsification of fat, salivary amylase's substrate, and where each food class is digested. All human digestion, C 3.2-LO-1.
Heart section labels, why arteries are thick-walled and veins valved, why the heart needs valves, and how leakage is prevented. Entirely human circulation, C 3.2-LO-2.
Excretory-system labels, the main toxic waste filtered, and two selectively reabsorbed substances. Human excretory pathway and organs, C 3.2-LO-2.
